title: Do the numbers measure what matters?

parts.title: Whose values?
parts.brief: Public versus patient values for the running example: adaptation lifts the untreated state's weight, the gain shrinks and the ICER rises; the case for each side.
parts.figure: The running example as quality-over-time profiles: quality weight q (0 to 1) against years (0 to 5). Standard care: a flat path at q = 0.5 for 4 years, labelled 'Standard care' with its area '2.0 QALYs'; new treatment: a flat path at q = 0.7 for 5 years, labelled 'New treatment', '3.5 QALYs'; the gap between them shaded as the gain, readout 'ΔQ = 1.5'. When patients' values are introduced, the standard-care path rises to q = 0.6 (illustrative), leaving a faded ghost at 0.5; its area now '2.4 QALYs', the shaded gain shrinks, readout 'ΔQ = 1.1'. The line with the two sides highlights first the ghost (public) and then the raised path (patients). Readout card: 'ICER 20,000 → ≈27,000' — temporary, gone after line 11. Quiz: A value set is built from patients who live with a condition, not from the public. For a treatment that cures that condition, the QALY gain is likely to… | Grow | Shrink | Stay the same | correct: 2 | wrong hint: Patients tend to rate their own state higher — how much is left to gain?
script: We have asked whether every QALY should count the same; now the harder question: do the numbers themselves measure what matters?
Take our 60-year-old: standard care, four years at a weight of 0.5 — two QALYs.
With the new treatment, five years at 0.7 — three and a half QALYs, a gain of 1.5.
But who said the untreated state is worth 0.5?
In the value sets NICE prefers, members of the general public did — people imagining the state, not living in it.
Patients who live with a condition tend to rate it higher than the public imagines it.
Part of that is adaptation: people adjust their goals, find new routines, and cope better than outsiders expect.
Suppose patients put the untreated state at 0.6 — an illustrative number.
Standard care is now worth 2.4 QALYs, and the gain shrinks from 1.5 to 1.1.
The same 30,000 now buys fewer QALYs: the ICER rises from 20,000 to about 27,000 per QALY.
The case for the public: they pay for the health service, and any of them could become the patient.
The case for patients: they know the state, and the public may imagine it far worse than it is.
And adaptation cuts both ways: counting it means less value in treating people who have learned to cope.
So the same patient's gain depends on whose judgement sets the weight.

parts.title: Same state, three methods
parts.brief: Visual analogue scale, time trade-off and standard gamble give the same state different weights, usually VAS < TTO < SG; why, and how payers fix one ruler.
parts.figure: A number line for the quality weight q from 0 ('Dead') to 1 ('Full health'). The untreated state from our example is placed three times, one point per method as it is named: 'VAS' at 0.4, 'TTO' at 0.5, 'SG' at 0.6 (illustrative positions), each labelled with its short name and value. The TTO point at 0.5 is marked as 'our 0.5'. When the reasons are given, each point is highlighted in turn (SG: risk aversion; TTO: time preference; VAS: no sacrifice). A bracket spanning 0.4 to 0.6 labelled 'same state' appears when the line says none is simply right. Quiz: A state is valued at 0.8 by standard gamble. Valued by time trade-off, the same people would most likely give it… | A higher weight | A lower weight | The same weight | correct: 2 | wrong hint: Think about what dislike of risk does to the gamble's number.
script: Now that we have seen whose values count, take one group of people and ask about the same state three ways.
On a visual analogue scale, they simply mark the state on a line from dead to full health, like a thermometer.
In a time trade-off, they give up years of life to live the rest in full health.
In a standard gamble, they accept a risk of death for a chance at full health.
For the same state, the numbers usually fall in the same order: the gamble highest, the trade-off next, the scale lowest.
Our 0.5 is a trade-off value; the scale might say 0.4, the gamble 0.6 — illustrative numbers.
The gamble comes out high because most people dislike risk: facing a chance of death, they cling to the state they know.
The trade-off has its own pull: distant years feel worth less, so people give more of them up, which pulls the weight down.
The scale asks for no sacrifice at all: it records a feeling about the state, not a choice.
None of the three is simply right; each builds its own assumption about risk and time into the weight.
Payers answer by fixing one method in advance — NICE uses EQ-5D values from time trade-off — so every drug is measured with the same ruler.
So a weight is not a fact about the state; it is the state seen through a method.

parts.title: What the questionnaire sees
parts.brief: The EQ-5D's five dimensions, what falls outside them (hearing, vision, some mental illness), the SF-6D disagreeing, children and carers; the strength of a short common form.
parts.figure: A thing with named parts: the EQ-5D drawn as a large frame (a window) holding five labelled boxes, drawn one by one: 'Mobility', 'Self-care', 'Activities', 'Pain', 'Anxiety / depression'. Outside the frame, dashed boxes appear for what it does not ask: 'Hearing', 'Vision', and a dashed 'Mental illness' tag half outside next to 'Anxiety / depression'. Scratch card beside the frame: 'SF-6D ≠ EQ-5D', 'floor above 0', 'worst states: higher', 'mild states: lower' — temporary, gone after line 7. Then outside the frame on the other side: a small child figure labelled 'Child' with a question mark (who values?), and a carer figure labelled 'Carer' beside the patient, outside the frame; a dashed arrow brings the carer in labelled 'NICE: if relevant'. At the strength line the five boxes are highlighted together ('5 questions'); at the bolt-on line a sixth dashed box 'Bolt-on' attaches to the frame. Quiz: A hearing-aid programme shows almost no QALY gain on the EQ-5D, though users say their lives are much better. What is the most likely reason? | Hearing aids do not work | The EQ-5D does not ask about hearing | The discount rate is too high | correct: 2 | wrong hint: Look at what the five questions ask about.
script: Now that we have seen methods move the weight, look at the questionnaire that feeds it.
The EQ-5D asks about five things: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain, and anxiety or depression.
Whatever it does not ask about, it cannot see.
Hearing loss and poor vision barely register, and in some mental illnesses the five questions miss much of what changes.
A different questionnaire, the SF-6D, gives different values for the same patients.
Its values cannot fall below zero, and compared with the EQ-5D it tends to rate the worst states higher and mild states lower.
So a trial's QALY gain can depend on which form the patients filled in.
Children are harder still: a young child cannot fill in the form, and adults must imagine a child's state to value it.
Carers sit outside the frame altogether: the spouse who loses sleep and work appears nowhere in the patient's QALYs.
NICE allows carers' health effects to be added when they are relevant, but analyses often leave them out.
Yet the narrowness is also the strength: five short questions, answered by anyone, in any trial, comparable across diseases.
Bolt-on questions, for hearing, vision or sleep, are one repair under study.
A QALY sees health through its questionnaire's window; whatever falls outside counts for nothing.

parts.title: The rivals
parts.brief: QALY, DALY, WELLBY and capability (ICECAP) side by side with a plus and a minus each; synthesis: a cost per QALY carries three choices; closing quiz.
parts.figure: A table filled in row by row, columns 'Measure', 'Counts', 'Plus', 'Minus'. Row 'QALY': 'health gained' | 'comparable' | 'health only'. Row 'DALY': 'health lost' | 'one global yardstick' | 'health, not choice'. Row 'WELLBY': 'life satisfaction' | 'beyond health' | 'adaptation counts'. Row 'ICECAP': 'capabilities' | 'freedom' | 'hard to trade'. Each row's cells appear as its lines are spoken, the Plus cell and then the Minus cell highlighted when each is said. Small scratch card for the DALY: 'YLL + YLD', '0 = full health, 1 = death' — temporary, gone after line 5. At the synthesis, the whole table dims and three short cues appear beneath: 'Whose values?', 'Which method?', 'Which questionnaire?'. Quiz: Two analyses of the same drug report 18,000 and 35,000 per QALY. Before calling one of them wrong, what should you check first? | Whose values, which method, which questionnaire | Which has the larger sample | Which was published later | correct: 1 | wrong hint: Think back over what moved our example's ICER in this lecture.
script: Now that we have seen what the QALY can and cannot see, here are its rivals, side by side.
The QALY counts health gained, weighted by preferences — comparable across any disease, but health only.
The DALY, the disability-adjusted life year, turns it around: it counts health lost, years of life lost plus years lived with disability.
Its disability weights run the other way, 0 for full health and 1 for death, and they underpin the Global Burden of Disease studies.
Its strength is one yardstick for every country; its weakness is that the weights judge health, not what people would give up for it.
The WELLBY counts life satisfaction: one point on a 0 to 10 scale, for one person, for one year.
It reaches beyond health, so a housing policy and a drug can be compared; Britain's Treasury has guidance for using it.
But it counts adaptation in full — the very issue we began with.
Capability measures such as ICECAP-O, for older people, ask what a person is able to do and be: attachment, security, role, enjoyment, control.
They value freedom rather than function, but there is no settled way yet to weigh them against years of life.
Each rival repairs one blind spot and opens another.
So a cost per QALY is not a fact about a drug: it carries a choice of whose values, which method, and which questionnaire.
Its strength is that those choices are written down, so they can be checked, changed and argued over in the open.
Read any ICER with those three questions, and you can see what the number measures — and what it leaves out.
